extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of religion; educated general readers interested in comparative religion and moral psychology
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical chapter comparing Christianity, Judaism, Buddhism, and Brahmanism with focus on asceticism, celibacy, monasticism, and the psychological origins of religious renunciation. Includes historical examples (Shakers, Essenes, Trappists) and reflections on conversion through suffering and tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual chastity/celibacy as a divine virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: In accordance with the Church view ... perpetual chastity is called a divine, heavenly, angelic virtue, and the obtaining of the assistance of divine grace for this end is made dependent upon earnest prayer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (canonical Church Fathers, Synodal and Papal instructions, Council of Trent) present perpetual chastity as the highest merit; contemporary Catholic periodicals (e.g., 'Der Katholik') reaffirm this as an enduring Catholic doctrine. Anti-pattern: treating celibacy as merely optional or secondary when, in this tradition, it is the meritorious ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virginity as the perfect state; marriage as a make-shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Virginity is for both (Paul and Hebrews) the perfect state, marriage only a make-shift for the weak, and only as such to be held inviolable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents this as a recurring early-Christian evaluative standard: highest moral effort directed to 'complete, material putting off of self.' Use of marriage is tolerated for those unable to attain the ascetic ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celibacy deducible from the teaching of Christ and Paul (distinguishing law from spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: We agree with the Abbé Zaccaria, who asserts that celibacy (not the law of celibacy) is before everything to be deduced from the teaching of Christ and the Apostle Paul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between juridical imposition (law) and spiritual ideal (celibacy as moral teaching). Implication: authentic Christian asceticism is grounded in Christ/Paul rather than merely ecclesiastical regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Testament as world-denying/pessimistic and opposed to Old Testament optimism
rubrics_metrics.description: In the New Testament the world is always spoken of as something to which one does not belong ... This agrees with the ascetic spirit of the denial of one's self and the overcoming of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames doctrinal evaluation: where the Old Testament (panta kala lian) is optimistic, the New Testament emphasizes renunciation and views the world as morally compromised. Use this contrast to interpret Christian doctrines and practices as essentially ascetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religions require a mythical vehicle to make abstract truth practical
rubrics_metrics.description: For these men there was everywhere required ... a mythical vehicle for it, as it were a receptacle, without which it would be lost and dissipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical criterion for successful religious transmission: abstract philosophical truth must be clothed in myth to guide the masses; philosophy presents the same truth 'sensu proprio' to a small, capable minority. Anti-pattern: expecting mass comprehension of purely abstract formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protestantism's elimination of asceticism results in degeneration toward optimism/rationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Protestantism, since it has eliminated asceticism and its central point, the meritoriousness of celibacy, has already given up the inmost kernel of Christianity ... degenerates into the doctrine of a loving father ... and thus is no Christianity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative standard for religious authenticity: retention of ascetic core vs. substitution by optimistic, moralistic interpretations. Use as a historical-philosophical critique of Protestant developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monasticism as methodical denial of the will and an institution of sublime description (but prone to abuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monasticism, that methodical denial of the will practised in common for the sake of mutual encouragement, is an institution of a sublime description, which, however, for this very reason is for the most part untrue to its spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: monasticism's value is in its earnest, renunciatory core (e.g., Trappists maintain perfection through profound earnestness). Scoring note: judge monastic orders by fidelity to denial-of-will ideal and exclusion of secondary ends; abuses reduce practical value even when theoretical ideal is high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celibate sects embody linked social practices (community of goods, no private property, strict discipline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To celibacy most of the other conditions link themselves on of themselves. There are no families, and therefore there is no private property, but community of goods. All are clothed alike ... idleness is not endured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive evaluative pattern: assess celibate communities not only by sexual abstinence but by related institutional features (communal property, uniform dress, labor discipline, novitiate testing). Examples: Shakers, Rappists, Essenes. Use presence/absence of these features to characterize authenticity and durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion to renunciation often follows violent personal suffering or confrontation with death
rubrics_metrics.description: This great and rapid change of the inmost being of man ... appears most frequently when, with full consciousness, he stands in the presence of a violent and certain death ... conversions ... completely transform men ... (examples: Abbé Rancé; executions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological criterion: the intensity of suffering or imminent death produces genuine renunciation ('denial of the will'). Use biographical or testimonial evidence (executions, sudden traumatic events) when assessing causes of religious conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic experience of tragedy can produce elevation akin to renunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: By considering what every emotional man experiences on beholding a tragedy ... when in the fifth act this happiness is entirely wrecked and shattered, he experiences a certain elevation of the soul ... This is the same thing ... as that which takes place ... in the feeling of our own fate when it is heavy misfortune that drives the man at last into the haven of entire resignation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of psychological mechanisms: pleasurable elevation from witnessing tragedy (art) models the process by which real suffering can lead to denial of the will. Use tragic literature and theater as evidence or vehicles for fostering renunciatory insight.
